kids.content: Carmona, in the early 18th century, was a part of Hacienda of Biñan, but inhabited by natives of Silang. Early settlers cleared the area, built their homes and tilled the land until a community was organized. As their population grew and there came a need to establish religious services, a decree issued on March 9, 1746 by Don Pedro Calderon Enriquez, declared that area of Hacienda of Biñan, a part of the mission town of Silang and became known as Barrio Latag. Historical accounts from the Arzobispado de Manila showed that, as early as 1823, a movement to separate from their Mother Town started. It was a long struggle, a competition of strength, courage, and wit, and finally, the brave people of Latag won their coveted dream - to become an independent town. By virtue of a decree issued by Gov. Gen. Ramon Montero of the Superior Gobierno de las Islas Filipinas, Latag became a town and was named Carmona on February 20, 1857.

Having been recognized as a municipality, the people of Carmona proved their worth. They tilled the soil and made it productive. To give everybody a fair chance, the agricultural land was considered communal and divided into parcels for distribution to family heads, who shall have the right to till for three (3) years, and in case of competition, an auction for such right shall be administered, known then as “Subasta delas Tierras Communales del Pueblo de Carmona”. The Subasta or auction became a lottery or “Sorteo” in response to the growing population and competition for the right to till the communal land.

list items.content: A. THE TRANSFORMATION In the early 90’s, the Municipality of Carmona was cited to be one of the priority areas for industrial development in the province. Huge capital

kids.content: outlays were then channeled to its local government for the development of industrial estates. This brought about a drastic transformation of its vast landscape into industrial parks. This rapid development and influx of manufacturing companies as locators led to profound changes in the lives of the ordinary people of Carmona.

The increase in municipal revenues and population growth led to Carmona’s reclassification as First Class Municipality in July 1996 and also categorized as a minor urban center in the province of Cavite.

BPO industries also started to take part in the continuously growing business community of Carmona. Foreign investments are still pouring in, as export-oriented industries move in high gear. Thanks to the sustained industrial peace, competitive labor force, and good governance of Carmona.
B. CARMONA MUNICIPAL MAYORSImage 1-1. Carmona Municipal Mayors

Marcelino Palma Clarito, “Ninoy” to his friends, became the town mayor of Carmona during the pre-war period. Before he became a mayor, he served as “Juez de Paz” of the town. He was married to Patricia Mapanoo with whom he has an only son they named Elfredo.

Marcelo “Celo” Reyes was the son of Juanita Dearoz and Gavino Reyes. He was born on January 15, 1880. He was a cattle raiser before he was elected as Municipal Mayor. He held the post for more than one term. He was married to Leoncia Paular and blessed with five children – Leonides, Adoracion, Librada, Estela and Marcelo Jr.

The son of Gavino Reyes and Juanita Dearoz, Martin Reyes fondly called by his friends and family “Ting” became the mayor of Carmona also during the pre-war times. He was married to Antonina Tolentino, a native of Biñan, Laguna with whom he had four children – Bernardino, Catalino, Paterno and Paquita.

Prudencio “Densio” Torres is listed as the third municipal mayor of Carmona during the pre-war. He was born in Carmona, Cavite and married to Fortunata Trinidad with whom he had 5 children namely: Pedro, Aquilino, Sulpicio, Luciano and an only girl they named Nene.

Juan R. Alumia was born on January 28, 1886 in Carmona, Cavite, to the couple Agustin Alumia and Maria Reyes. A lawyer before becoming a mayor, he married Encarnacion Anulat with whom he had a daughter, Milagros. He died on December 12, 1969 at the age of 83.

Listed sixth in the line of mayors of Carmona, Estanislao Paular or “Islaw” to his friends and town folks was a sugarcane planter before being elected as a Mayor. He was born in Biñan, Laguna to the couple Potenciana Dico and Gavino Paular. He married Maria Nieves de Salit and was blessed with 9 children namely: Dominador, Lolita, Elisa, Lauro, Alfredo, Alberto, Emelita, Rogelio and Estrella.

Marciano “Anong” Mapanoo was born on January 1, 1904 in Carmona, Cavite to the couple Perpetuo Mapanoo and Ma. Cristina Papa Mapanoo. He married Asuncion Tuimaon with whom he had four children – Generoso, Santos, Montano and Marciano, Jr. Before he became the mayor of Carmona, he worked as a farmer and a sugar cane contractor. He was killed on February 8, 1944, few years after his term as mayor.

The son of Geronimo Hebron and Maxima Gutierez, Candido Hebron Sr. was born on June 3, 1903 in Carmona, Cavite. “Idong” as he was fondly called was married to Constancia Martillano with whom he had four sons namely Porfirio, Regalado, Geronimo and Candido, Jr. Before he became the Municipal Mayor, he worked as a lawyer. He also served as Municipal Treasurer during the administration of Mayor Cesar E. Casal. He died on December 12, 1969.

Juan Peñano Zamora was the only son of Gaudencio Zamora and Catalina Peñano. He was born on March 8, 1892 in Carmona, Cavite. Most people called him “Lugaw” because he used to harvest produce in big volumes giving him income more than their family needs. He was married to Valentina Cortez with whom he had nine (9) children - Ruperto, Remedios, Vicente, Virginia, Prospero, Concepcion, Araceli and the twins Lourdes and Maria. He died on June 14, 1978.

“Edong” as his family and colleagues called him was born on December 25, 1904 in Carmona, Cavite. He was married to Juliana Restrivera and had an only child they named Purificacion who proved to be a loving and caring daughter. Aside from being a concerned leader of this town, he worked as Supervisor in the Manila Water Service System (MWSS) and Secretary of the Municipal Government of Carmona. He died on June 3, 1981.

Arsenio Mapalad was born on October 18, 1897. He was married to Florentina Caloya and had seven (7) children namely Bartola, Placida, Florencia, Filomina, Elito, Azarias and Lea. He served in the military before he became the Municipal Mayor of Carmona in 1945.

Bernardo Bunda Hebron, Jr. also known as “Dandong” was the son of Bernardo Hebron Sr. and Mercedes Bunda. He was born March 12, 1910 in Carmona, Cavite and worked as a farmer and caretaker of their own rice mill before he became the mayor of Carmona. He was married to Simeona Reyes Levardo with whom he had eight (8) children – Perla, Norma, Adonis, Mirasol, Rodolfo, Wilfredo, Bienvenido and Bernardo.

The son of Andres Reyes, Eulalio Reyes served as the chief of police of the town and later on elected as mayor of Carmona. He was also a lawyer before he became the mayor of the town. He died on the 12th of December, 1969.

The son of Martiñano Casal and Magdalena Ermitaño, Cesar E. Casal was born in Sta. Ana, Manila. He was the longest serving mayor of Carmona. Married to Pilar Casal but their marriage was not blessed with children. He was a farmer, CPA and a lawyer when he became a mayor. After his term as Municipal Mayor, he was elected as Cavite Provincial Board Member for three consecutive terms.

Felino Maquinay was born on February 3, 1933 to the couple Dominador and Josefa Maquinay. He was married to Felisa Hernandez and was blessed with two (2) children namely Dorie and Herminio. He served as Municipal Mayor of Carmona for two consecutive terms. Shortly after celebrating his 57th birthday he was shot to death.

Estelito Torres also called “Ito” was born on September 3, 1943 in Carmona to Pedro and Miguela Torres, a resident of Silang, Cavite. He was married to Dr. Lualhati Salazar with whom they nurtured three (3) children - Cherry, Ritchie and Dennis. He was then an electrician and a contractor.

Rolando C. Rosas was the town’s vice-mayor when the then mayor Felino Maquinay died in 1990. He automatically assumed mayorship and continued his service until 1995. He was born on the 15th of November 1939 in Carmona to Segundino Rosas and Remy Clarito. He served as a policeman before becoming a ViceMayor. He is married to Teresita Capuso of Sta. Rosa, Laguna with whom he has five (5) children namely: Redentor, Rey, Diosdado, Rommel and Mutya. At present, he serves as a consultant in the local government.

Dr. Dahlia A. Loyola is the 8th Mayor of Carmona after the Commonwealth period. She is the 1st woman mayor, already elected to three (3) terms. Her 1st term is from 2004-2007, followed by two (2) consecutive terms from 2010 to 2019, taking her most trusted and reliable Mayor of the Town. At present, Dr. Dahlia is the Representative of the Fifth District of Cavite, making her the first woman representative of Carmona, Silang and GMA. She was born on the 26th of January, 1961 in Manila. Her parents are Engr. Epifanio R. Ambayec, a Civil Engineer, and Mrs. Milagros AlumiaAmbayec, a retired teacher. She is married to Atty. Roy M. Loyola, the former Congressional Representative of the 5th District of Cavite and presently the Municipal Mayor of Carmona. They are blessed with three children namely: Bea, Roy, Jr. and Roy III.

Dr. Dahlia studied elementary and secondary education in Colegio de Sta. Catalina de Sena, Biñan, Laguna and finished BS Zoology at the University of the Philippines, Los Baños, Laguna. She pursued Medical School at the University of Perpetual Help System Laguna and after a year-long internship at the AFP Medical Center (1986-1987), she passed the Medical Board Examination given in January 1988.
An advocate of peace, health, education, and women empowerment, she founded the Carmona Peace and Order

Foundation Inc., instituted the Association of Women for Carmona Development Inc., and spearheaded numerous activities and programs promoting the general welfare of the citizens of Carmona. Dr. Dahlia is the current President of the Cavite Mayors League and Board Director of the Philippine Red CrossCavite Chapter.

The Honorable Mayor Atty. Roy “Bobby” Loyola is one of the sons of Angelo Levardo Loyola, a District Supervisor, and Francisca Maulanin, a dedicated teacher. Born on February 17, 1962 in Carmona, he served as the town mayor for 12 years where under his administration Carmona transformed from agricultural community to an industrial zone hosting industrial parks and estates.

He finished his elementary and secondary education in Colegio de Sta. Catalina de Sena in Biñan, Laguna and studied college in the Philippine Christian University-Manila, completed his course, BS Business Administration. He then pursued Bachelor of Laws in the University of the East and has the distinction of being part of the 17% Bar passers out of 2,682 examinees during the 1987 Bar exams.

He is married to Dr. Dahlia Ambayec-Loyola and blessed with three children namely: Bea, Roy, Jr. and Roy III. After serving three consecutive terms from 2010-2019 as the Congressional Representative of the 5th District of Cavite, comprised of Carmona, GMA, and Silang, he is now back to serve the Carmonians as the Municipal Mayor.

list items.content: A.3. LAND CLASSIFICATION The Municipality of Carmona has a total land area of 3,092 hectares representing 2.18% of the total land area of Cavite. Based on the Political

kids.content: Boundary Survey conducted by the DENR on 2013, the total land area of Carmona is 2,967.8 hectares which is lower than the 3,092 land area that the municipality is using on the previous years (see table below). Carmona has no unclassified lands. No declared forest, mineral and public parks. But there are heritage lands with an area of 204 hectares agri-land owned by the people of Carmona and administered by the Local Government Unit of Carmona. National Government Agencies are now using the new land area of Carmona set by the DENR as their basis for planning and budgeting. Presently, the LGUCarmona is using the old land area since the approved CLUP (2011-2022) is based on the 3,092 hectare lot but will be updated with this new CLUP (2023-onwards).

Carmona has an elevation of about 11 to 212 meters or 36 to 695 feet above sea level. The lowest elevation is Barangay Maduya and Poblacion Areas (Barangay 1–8), while Barangay Cabilang Baybay, the northern part of Mabuhay, Milagrosa and Lantic are at a median elevation. The southern part of Milagrosa is situated at the highest altitude of the municipality, along with Barangay Bancal and the rest of Barangay Mabuhay and Lantic.

Based on the Philippine Geographic Information System (GIS), there are six slope classifications. In Carmona, only four slopes exist, ranging from 0 (level to nearly level) to 30% (rolling to moderately steep). These slopes are classified to indicate the probable limits of various types of land uses. Category A (areas that are level to nearly level) comprised mostly the eastern half of Carmona. Under this category is the lowland part of Carmona, including the Barangays of Maduya, Poblacion, and Milagrosa extending up to the steep boundaries of Lantic, Mabuhay, and Cabilang Baybay. Meanwhile, the western half represents the highland portion of Carmona, which includes Barangays Lantic, Bancal, and Mabuhay.

list items.content: E.1. CURRENT CLIMATE Carmona is under Type I climate characterized by two (2) pronounced seasons: dry from November to April and wet during the rest of the year.

kids.content: Maximum rainfall usually occurs from June to September. The average annual rainfall is 200 millimeters with a peak of 400 millimeters in August.

list items.content: G.1. WATER RESOURCES Carmona falls within the Biñan River Basin as well as the Laguna de Bay Region Administrative Jurisdiction. It covers an area of about 81 sq. kms

kids.content: with an area of about 81 sq. kms, with an annual rainfall depth over the basin estimated at 2, 637 millimeters and an annual surface run-off depth of 1, 166 mm. Surface water resources of Carmona is sourced from rivers such as the Carmona River, Soro-soro, Calabuso, Cahilan, Manawa, Embarkadero, Asuntoy and Pasong Pare as well as from springs in particular Bucal and the Munting Ilog Spring. The river systems of Carmona are connected to the rivers of Silang and Dasmariñas and empty towards Laguna de Bay. Carmona rivers and its tributaries are being used as source of water for irrigation purposes. Munting Ilog Spring in Silang flows down to Munting Ilog in Carmona. Munting Ilog Spring and Carmona River irrigate the agricultural areas of Lantic, Ligdang and Maduya. The Lantic dam located in Barangay Lantic which is composed of Prinsang Luma and Prinsang Bago derive its water supply from the Carmona River.

The groundwater of Carmona has an average well depth of 116 meters, average static level of 52 meters below ground surface and average specific capacity of 0.24 liters per second per meter of drawdown (NWRDB Rapid Assessment of Water Supply for Cavite, 1982). As part of the larger Biñan River Basin, the groundwater of Carmona is characterized as having a recharge of about 8 mcm per year and an annual discharge of 39 mcm. Groundwater pumpage for the whole basin is computed at 10 mcm per year.

Today, some areas like Cabilang Baybay and other parts of Poblacion have been depending on the Carmona Water District for water supply as potable water cannot be drawn from the average 52 meters below the ground surface. Instead, submersible pumps are the only way to draw water at 300 meters. It should be noted that based on the same study, the groundwater of Carmona decreases almost a meter every year and is expected to reach its limit by 2015. Hence, it is crucial to determine possible alternative water resources that can be utilized by the people in the future.

One of the strategies that the LGU will undertake to provide the residents of Carmona with alternative water resources is through the conduct of the Carmona River Profiling, which might be used by the LGU for future planning activities. This initiative will help the LGU establish its updated natural water systems inventory and baseline information that will later be of great importance in transforming the 30% of the municipality’s natural water systems to Class C for domestic, commercial, recreational, and industrial by 2022.

The literacy rate can be classified as Functional Literacy, Simple Literacy, and High Literacy. Functional literacy is defined as the ability to read, write, and perform simple mathematical calculations. Simple or Basic Literacy, on the other hand, is the ability of persons age 10 years old and above to read, write and understand simple messages in any language or dialect. Lastly, High literacy is the ability of using the written word (and making simple arithmetic calculations) in daily life, and to continue learning.

Currently, there are 1,606 illiterate persons in the municipality or 2.15% of the population. It is above the 91.6% national literacy rate. list items.content: A. AGRICULTURAL LANDS AFFECTED BY FLOODING Based on the climate and disaster risk assessment (natural resource-based production area), Barangays Maduya, Cabilang Baybay and Bancal are

list items.content: A. TRANSPORTATION Carmona is accessible thru land travel from all directions. It is at the crossroads from north to south between Cavite and Laguna as well as the

kids.content: gateway to the southern provinces of the region and beyond. From Carmona Public Market Terminal, Jeepney routes from Carmona to Biñan and GMA/Dasmariñas are available via the provincial road Governor’s Drive and the National Highway. Bus and Jeepney trips to Alabang, Manila and Calamba are available going thru the South Expressway and Biñan thru the national roads. San Pedro, Laguna is also accessible thru Southwoods Drive in Barangay Cabilang-Baybay while the inner barangays of Biñan, Laguna, Laguna Technopark and Laguna International Industrial Park (LIIP) may be accessed thru Dahlia Street and Mayor’s Boulevard. Tagaytay is accessed thru Maguyam Road which connects to Aguinaldo Highway in Silang, Cavite.

The average travel time within a 30-kilometer zone is about 30 minutes without traffic. Increasing traffic volume has made trips in all direction longer than the normal travel time due to the limited carrying capacity of the major road systems. New access points to and from the municipality is a priority and several old roads have been improved while new ones are laid to provide additional access. The old Sugar road is a good choice for a new north-south access via Southwoods Drive and South Expressway to Sta. Rosa and Canlubang via Loma in Biñan, Laguna. The rough road of Paligawan is also an ideal route going to Silang and Tagaytay City if it could be connected to Sugar road and/or Mayor’s Boulevard. Another South Express exit linking Mayor’s Boulevard is another alternative considered to ease the huge traffic at the Carmona South Luzon Expressway (SLEX) toll exit during rush hours. Currently, in 2020, the current interchange has a total average daily interchange traffic of 34,820 vehicles per day, and it is estimated that by 2040 it will be 127,591 as the municipality and the municipalities and cities around Carmona develop.

As Carmona is a major commuter artery to and from Cavite, Biñan, Laguna, new commuter infrastructure is being explored to increase service quality, reduce road congestion, and increase economic development for the municipality. Digitizing the transport layer through technology that will help route planning, estimated times, and infrastructure development is a focus of the municipality.

Local transportation is also a priority of the municipality, with a focus on encouraging the use of bikes and walking, possibly through mixed-use development. Electric vehicle infrastructure is also going to be promoted with new and current developments to reduce carbon dioxide and other toxic fumes and the level of noise pollution in the municipality.

list items.content: A.3. FLOOD CONTROL AND DRAINAGE FACILITIES Most of the barangays have existing storm drainage systems running along the streets of the municipality. It consists mainly of reinforced concrete

kids.content: pipes, lined and unlined open canals and reinforced concrete rectangular culvert or the box type canals. Since Poblacion area is prone to flooding due to the natural grade of the area and the lack of planning during the 70’s, 80’s and 90’s developments, the municipality embarked on a comprehensive program of developing a drainage system that can cope with the fast-growing problem of flooding during the late 90’s up to present. The municipality has now two (2) main storm drainage pipes that can handle vast amount of storm water. One is the 245-meter long, 1.5-2 meter-diameter underground pipe along Purificacion Street. It runs from the existing creek in Barangays 7 and 8 draining to the Carmona River. The other drainage pipe is the 120-meter long, 2-meter-diameter underground pipe along Tenedero Street running from Magallanes Street and draining to the existing creek in Barangay 2 which eventually drains to Carmona River.

Initiated flood control projects include the construction of the Drainage System at Phase 2, Brgy. 8, Hebron St., Brgy. Mabuhay and Carmona National High School (CNHS). Also, there has been a rehabilitation/improvement of canal at Mapalad St., Brgy. Mabuhay and construction of Drainage System (Box Culvert) at Brgy. 8. Despite the increase in the inventory of drainages in the municipality, the construction of effective drainage and flood control system is still needed, particularly at Phase 4, Patindig Araw, which has a relatively small size of drainage concrete pipes that resulted to continuous flooding due to clogged drainages.

The total length of the municipality’s drainage system is 146.93 km. of which 6.67 km or 5% is covered with concrete hollow blocks (CHB), 20.48 km or 14% are open CHB, 89.83 km or 61% is reinforced concrete pipe (RCP). However, there are still 29 km of road in some barangays that have no drainage canals especially in parts of Barangays 3, 4, 6, 7 and 10.

Currently, there is a proposal to open new bridges to connect Sugar Road to Lankiwa Road in Biñan as well as a road linking Mag-asawang Mangga in Governor’s Drive to MJC access road.
